{"content":"1|#!/bin/sh
2|# Restore only receipt-selected existing roots after Incus readiness. Numbered
3|# names are selectors, never identity authority. Preflight all boot selections
4|# before restoring anything; conflicting logical identities fail closed.
5|# This base-owned service is not installed/enabled by application activation.
6|exec 2>&1
7|rm -f /run/opdbus/runit-ready/identity-roots
8|fail() { printf 'identity-roots: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
9|secure_path() (
10|    path=$1
11|    [ "$(realpath -e -- "$path")" = "$path" ] || fail "noncanonical path: $path"
12|    while :; do
13|        [ ! -L "$path" ] && [ "$(stat -c %u -- "$path")" = 0 ] &&
14|            [ $((0$(stat -c %a -- "$path") & 022)) -eq 0 ] || fail "unsafe owner/mode: $path"
15|        [ "$path" != / ] || break
16|        path=$(dirname -- "$path")
17|    done
18|)
19|private_receipt() {
20|    secure_path "$1" || return 1
21|    [ -f "$1" ] && [ "$(stat -c %u:%g:%a "$1")" = 0:0:600 ]
22|}
23|wait_dep() {
24|    sv start "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
25|    i=0
26|    until sv check "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do
27|        i=$((i + 1))
28|        [ "$i" -ge 90 ] && fail "dependency $1 not ready after 90s"
29|        sleep 1
30|    done
31|}
32|wait_dep incus
33|i=0
34|until incus info >/dev/null 2>&1; do
35|    i=$((i + 1))
36|    [ "$i" -lt 60 ] || fail 'incusd API not ready'
37|    sleep 1
38|done
39|# Deliberate release-owned dependency selection; a partial/broken activated
40|# closure is an error, not permission to execute an older base helper.
41|if [ "${OP_IDENTITY_HELPER_DIR+x}" = x ]; then
42|    helper_dir=$OP_IDENTITY_HELPER_DIR
43|else
44|    helper_dir=/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers
45|fi
46|helper_dir=$(realpath -e -- "$helper_dir") || fail 'selected helper directory absent'
47|secure_path "$helper_dir" || exit 1
48|for dependency in op-identity-root op-identity-image restore-chatbot-root sync-instance-upgrade runit-ready-signal; do
49|    secure_path "$helper_dir/$dependency" || exit 1
50|    [ -f "$helper_dir/$dependency" ] && [ -x "$helper_dir/$dependency" ] || fail "selected helper unavailable: $dependency"
51|done
52|helper=$helper_dir/op-identity-root
53|restore_helper=$helper_dir/restore-chatbot-root
54|# Keep the entire root-helper chain in the selected closure.
55|OP_IDENTITY_IMAGE_HELPER=$helper_dir/op-identity-image
56|OP_SYNC_INSTANCE_UPGRADE_HELPER=$helper_dir/sync-instance-upgrade
57|export OP_IDENTITY_IMAGE_HELPER OP_SYNC_INSTANCE_UPGRADE_HELPER
58|chatbot_session=b0c777e3-0955-cd8b-3d01-ca12998cae28
59|physical=${OP_IDENTITY_SEED_STATE:-/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/seed-identities}
60|legacy=${IDENTITIES:-/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/identities}
61|gpt_present=0
62|gpt_name=
63|physical_present=0
64|physical_names=
65|selected_sessions='|'
66|# GPT boot receipts attest completed adoption; restore --check verifies exact
67|# native UUID/session/key plus the corresponding private disk/root receipts.
68|# ID-N fails closed here: no offline authority validator, no live-bridge boot dependency.
69|# Never execute restoration while another receipt could name the same chatbot.
70|for receipt in /var/lib/3tched-leaf-pool/.provisioning/*.boot.json; do
71|    [ -e "$receipt" ] || [ -L "$receipt" ] || continue
72|    gpt_present=1
73|    private_receipt "$receipt" || fail "unsafe GPT boot receipt: $receipt"
74|    name=$(basename "$receipt" .boot.json)
75|    [ -z "$gpt_name" ] || fail 'multiple GPT chatbot boot receipts; reconcile before restoration'
76|    "$restore_helper" --check "$name" || fail "invalid GPT chatbot boot receipt: $name"
77|    gpt_name=$name
78|    selected_sessions="$selected_sessions$chatbot_session|"
79|done
80|for receipt in "$physical"/*/state.json; do
81|    [ -e "$receipt" ] || [ -L "$receipt" ] || continue
82|    physical_present=1
83|    name=$(basename "$(dirname "$receipt")")
84|    marker=$physical/$name/boot-ready.json
85|    if [ ! -e "$marker" ] && [ ! -L "$marker" ]; then
86|        echo "physical seed $name: no authoritative-completion boot opt-in; skipped"
87|        continue
88|    fi
89|    private_receipt "$receipt" && private_receipt "$marker" || fail "unsafe physical boot receipts: $name"
90|    # Keep existing canonical UUID roots and the legacy chatbot alias. Reject
91|    # numbered selections before any restoration: online canonical replay is
92|    # operator-only, and no offline authoritative boot validator exists yet.
93|    jq -e --arg name "$name" --arg sid "$chatbot_session" '
94|        .version==1 and .layout=="shared-partition-siblings-v2" and .name==$name and .phase=="ready" and
95|        (.session|type=="string" and test("^[0-9a-f]{8}(-[0-9a-f]{4}){3}-[0-9a-f]{12}$")) and
96|        (.instance_uuid|type=="string" and test("^[0-9a-f]{8}(-[0-9a-f]{4}){3}-[0-9a-f]{12}$")) and
97|        (.session==$name or (.session==$sid and $name=="3tchedChatbot"))
98|    ' "$receipt" >/dev/null || fail "invalid/incomplete physical boot receipt: $name"
99|    policy=$(jq -er '.start_on_boot|select(type=="boolean")|tostring' "$marker") || fail "invalid physical boot policy: $name"
100|    expected=$(jq -cS --argjson start "$policy" '{version,layout,image,members,persist,name,session,instance_uuid,root,seed_fsid,seed_generation,sprout_fsid,leaf,leaf_inode,leaf_size,start_on_boot:$start}' "$receipt") || fail "invalid storage pins: $name"
101|    actual=$(jq -cS . "$marker") || fail "invalid boot marker: $name"
102|    [ "$expected" = "$actual" ] || fail "physical boot/storage pins differ: $name"
103|    session=$(jq -er .session "$receipt") || fail "missing physical session: $name"
104|    case "$selected_sessions" in
105|        *"|$session|"*) fail "conflicting boot receipts for logical identity $session; no roots restored" ;;
106|    esac
107|    selected_sessions="$selected_sessions$session|"
108|    physical_names="$physical_names $name"
109|done
110|failed=0
111|if [ -n "$gpt_name" ]; then
112|    "$restore_helper" "$gpt_name" || failed=$((failed + 1))
113|fi
114|seed_readonly_ready=0
115|for name in $physical_names; do
116|    receipt=$physical/$name/state.json
117|    marker=$physical/$name/boot-ready.json

10|[[ $name != ID-* || $action != boot ]] || fail 'numbered boot requires offline authoritative binding validation; online canonical replay is operator-only'

84|    ' <<<"$instance" >/dev/null || fail 'native chatbot UUID/session/key differs'

260|    # The client checks the typed mode as well; capture the declared host SID

262|    expected_session=${OP_3TCHEDFS_EXPECTED_SESSION:-$(jq -er '.session_id|select(type=="string" and length>0)' "$lungs_mount/.3tchedfs.json")}
263|    pin=$(namespace_pin) || die 'operator namespace unavailable'
264|    jq -e --arg sid "$expected_session" '.session_id==$sid' "$lungs_mount/.3tchedfs.json" >/dev/null || die 'operator session differs'
265|    assert_namespace() {
266|        local current
267|        current=$(namespace_pin) || die 'operator namespace lost; do not retry an uncertain operation'
268|        [[ $current == "$pin" ]] || die 'operator namespace changed; reconcile before retrying'
269|    }
270|    read_instances() {
271|        local state
272|        assert_namespace
273|        # The declared public projection intentionally redacts names/config and
274|        # devices. Never widen it or invent a get/list plugin method. Read the
275|        # same local default-project provider for this host maintenance tool.
276|        state=$(timeout --kill-after=5s 30s incus --force-local --project default query '/1.0/instances?recursion=1') || die 'bounded native instance readback failed'
277|        jq -e 'type=="array" and all(.[]; type=="object" and (.name|type=="string"))' <<<"$state" >/dev/null || die 'invalid native inventory'
278|        assert_namespace
279|        printf '%s\n' "$state"
280|    }
281|    incus_call() {
282|        local method=$1 args=$2 receipt
283|        assert_namespace
284|        receipt=$(timeout --kill-after=5s 30s "$client" invoke --mount "$lungs_mount" --expected-session "$expected_session" \
285|            --confirm-side-effects --args "$args" "plugins/incus/operations/$method/call") || return "$?"
286|        assert_namespace
287|        jq -ce --arg method "$method" 'select(.plugin_id=="incus" and .method==$method) |
288|            .result | select(.success==true and .outcome=="completed" and .plugin_id=="incus" and .method==$method) | .result' <<<"$receipt"
289|    }
290|    # Label is only a local durable retry fence and display metadata. It is NOT
291|    # a requested native name. Preserve the exact request/caller before invoke.
292|    label=$SYSTEM_NAME
293|    umask 077
294|    directory=${OP_SYSTEM_PROVISION_RECEIPTS:-/var/lib/opdbus-runtime/system-provision-receipts}
295|    [[ $directory == /* && $(realpath -m "$directory") == "$directory" && ! -L $directory ]] || die 'unsafe system receipt directory'
296|    root_path "$(dirname "$directory")"
297|    [[ -e $directory ]] || mkdir -m 0700 "$directory"
298|    root_path "$directory"
299|    [[ -d $directory && $(stat -c %a "$directory") == 700 ]] || die 'system receipt directory must be private'
300|    intent=$directory/$label.json
301|    [[ ! -L $directory/$label.lock ]] || die 'unsafe system creation lock'
302|    exec 9>"$directory/$label.lock"
303|    flock -n 9 || die 'system creation active'
304|    create_args=$(jq -cn --arg op "$OPERATION_ID" --arg label "$label" --arg image "$IMAGE" --arg pool "$SYSTEM_STORAGE" \
305|        '{operation_id:$op,image:$image,source_mode:"image",instance_type:"container",profiles:[],
306|          config:{"user.display_name":$label,"security.privileged":"false","security.nesting":"false","boot.autostart":"false"},
307|          devices:[{name:"root",device:{type:"disk",path:"/",pool:$pool}}]}')
308|    if [[ -e $intent || -L $intent ]]; then

310|        [[ -f $intent && ! -L $intent && $(stat -c %a "$intent") == 600 ]] || die 'unsafe system intent'
311|        jq -e --argjson args "$create_args" --arg caller "$expected_session" \
312|            '.args==$args and .caller_session==$caller' "$intent" >/dev/null ||
313|            die 'retained label uses another operation/request/caller; reconcile it, never allocate a fresh ID'
314|    else
315|        tmp=$(mktemp "$directory/.create.XXXXXX")
316|        jq -n --argjson args "$create_args" --arg caller "$expected_session" \
317|            '{version:1,phase:"create-intent",args:$args,caller_session:$caller}' > "$tmp"
318|        sync -f "$tmp"; ln "$tmp" "$intent"; rm -- "$tmp"; sync -f "$directory"
319|    fi

323|        (.native_uuid|type=="string" and test("^[0-9a-f]{8}(-[0-9a-f]{4}){3}-[0-9a-f]{12}$"))

325|    SYSTEM_NAME=$(jq -er .name <<<"$created")
326|    native_uuid=$(jq -er .native_uuid <<<"$created")
327|    if jq -e 'has("result")' "$intent" >/dev/null; then

329|    fi

332|    sync -f "$tmp"; mv -T "$tmp" "$intent"; sync -f "$directory"

342|            .config["boot.autostart"]=="false" and

27|## Identity

32|| **CLI tool** | `btrfs` (subcommands: `filesystem`, `subvolume`, `balance`, `scrub`, `device`, `quota`, `qgroup`, `check`, `defragment`, `rescue`) |

37|## Quick Start
38|
39|```bash
40|sudo apt install btrfs-progs
41|sudo mkfs.btrfs -L mydata /dev/sdX1
42|sudo mount /dev/sdX1 /mnt/mydata

47|## Key Operations
48|
49|| Task | Command |
50||------|---------|
51|| Show filesystems | `btrfs filesystem show` |
52|| Filesystem usage (detailed) | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` |
53|| List subvolumes | `btrfs subvolume list /mount` |
54|| Create subvolume | `btrfs subvolume create /mount/name` |
55|| Delete subvolume | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/name` |
56|| Create read-write snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/src /mount/dst` |
57|| Create read-only snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot -r /mount/src /mount/dst` |
58|| Rollback: delete current, rename snapshot | `btrfs subvolume delete /mount/@; mv /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
59|| Rollback: recreate subvolume from snapshot | `btrfs subvolume snapshot /mount/@snapshot /mount/@` |
60|| Balance start (all chunks) | `btrfs balance start /mount` |
61|| Balance start (metadata only) | `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
62|| Balance status | `btrfs balance status /mount` |
63|| Balance cancel | `btrfs balance cancel /mount` |
64|| Scrub start | `btrfs scrub start /mount` |
65|| Scrub status | `btrfs scrub status /mount` |
66|| Scrub cancel | `btrfs scrub cancel /mount` |
67|| Check filesystem (read-only) | `btrfs check /dev/sdX` (unmounted) |
68|| Defragment file or directory | `btrfs filesystem defragment -r /mount` |
69|| Resize (grow) | `btrfs filesystem resize max /mount` |
70|| Resize (shrink) | `btrfs filesystem resize -10G /mount` |
71|| Add device | `btrfs device add /dev/sdY /mount` |
72|| Remove device | `btrfs device remove /dev/sdY /mount` |
73|| Device read/write error stats | `btrfs device stats /mount` |
74|| Enable quotas | `btrfs quota enable /mount` |
75|| Show qgroup usage | `btrfs qgroup show -reF /mount` |

77|## Expected State
78|
79|- `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters are `0` (any non-zero value is a read/write error)
80|- `btrfs scrub status /mount` → `Status: finished` with `0 errors`
81|- `btrfs balance status /mount` → `No balance found on '/mount'` when idle
82|- `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → Data and metadata ratios show reasonable allocation (metadata should not be >80% full)
83|
84|## Health Checks
85|
86|1. `btrfs device stats /mount` → all counters `0`; any non-zero value means hardware errors, act immediately
87|2. `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` → check both Data and Metadata sections; metadata ENOSPC is the most common silent failure
88|3. `btrfs scrub status /mount` → verify last scrub completed with no errors; schedule scrubs monthly via systemd timer or cron
89|4. `btrfs subvolume list /mount` → audit snapshot count; accumulation fills disk without appearing in normal `df` output
90|
91|## Common Failures
92|
93|| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
94||---------|-------|-----|
95|| `no space left on device` but `df` shows free space | Metadata chunks exhausted while data chunks exist | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — run `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to rebalance underused chunks |
96|| RAID-1 on data but single on metadata | Dangerous default when adding a second disk; metadata is not redundant | `btrfs filesystem usage /mount` — check metadata profile; run `btrfs balance start -mconvert=raid1 /mount` |
97|| Filesystem mounts read-only | Encountered an error it cannot self-correct | Check `dmesg | grep -i btrfs`; run `btrfs check /dev/sdX` on unmounted device to assess damage |
98|| Balance fails with ENOSPC mid-run | Not enough free space to relocate all chunks | Use `-dusage=<N>` filter to relocate only partially-used chunks first; free up space before retrying |
99|| Qgroup show reports inflated usage | Qgroups track snapshot references — shared data counted in each | Shared data is expected; use `btrfs qgroup show -reF` to see exclusive vs shared bytes |
100|| Snapshot accumulation fills disk | Old snapshots reference deleted data, preventing space reclaim | `btrfs subvolume list /mount | grep snapshot` — delete old snapshots with `btrfs subvolume delete` |
101|| `btrfs check --repair` made it worse | `--repair` is not safe for general use and can corrupt data | Never run `--repair` without consulting upstream; use `rescue` subcommands instead |
102|| Filesystem errors after kernel upgrade | Older on-disk format or regression | Check `dmesg`; downgrade kernel or use `btrfs rescue` tools; check known issues for your kernel version |
103|
104|## Pain Points
105|
106|- **ENOSPC due to metadata/data imbalance**: The most common Btrfs "gotcha". Btrfs allocates space in chunks — if metadata chunks fill up, writes fail even when data chunks are available and `df` still shows free space. Fix: `btrfs balance start -dusage=50 /mount` to reclaim partially-empty chunks. This is not a bug — it is the expected behavior when chunk allocation becomes imbalanced.
107|- **Mixed RAID profiles between data and metadata**: Adding a second disk does not automatically mirror metadata. A system can have `RAID1` data but `single` metadata, meaning metadata loss on one disk is fatal. Always explicitly set both with `-d` and `-m` flags.
108|- **Snapshots are instant but they accumulate**: Snapshot creation is O(1) and free. Deletion requires reference counting and can be slow. Unreferenced snapshots hold on to deleted data indefinitely — disk usage only decreases after snapshot deletion completes.
109|- **`btrfs check` is slow and `--repair` is risky**: Unlike `fsck.ext4`, Btrfs check does not have a safe repair mode. `--repair` can corrupt a filesystem that `check` reports as damaged. Prefer `btrfs rescue` subcommands (`zero-log`, `fix-device-size`) for targeted fixes.
110|- **Btrfs RAID-5/6 has known parity issues**: As of kernels through 6.x, Btrfs RAID-5 and RAID-6 have unresolved write-hole bugs. Do not use RAID-5/6 for data you care about. Use RAID-1 or RAID-10 instead.
111|- **Send/receive for backups**: `btrfs send` / `btrfs receive` is efficient for incremental backups using read-only snapshots as base references. Tools like `snapper` and `btrbk` automate the snapshot lifecycle and send/receive workflow — prefer them over manual scripting.
112|- **CoW fragmentation on databases and VMs**: Copy-on-write writes new data to new locations, which fragments sequential files over time. Use `nodatacow` mount option (or `chattr +C`) for VM disk images, database files, and other large randomly-written files. `nodatacow` also disables checksums for those files.
113|
114|## See Also
115|
116|- **ext4** — Traditional Linux filesystem without CoW overhead; use when you need maximum compatibility and don't need snapshots
117|- **xfs** — High-performance filesystem for large sequential I/O; use for databases and media workloads where CoW fragmentation is a concern
118|- **zfs** — Full storage stack with pooling and replication; use when you need enterprise-grade checksums and send/receive without kernel version sensitivity

15|

17|## Quick Navigation
18|
19|- [references/stack_allocations.md](references/stack_allocations.md)

21|
22|# Rust Memory Optimization Guide
23|
24|Advanced strategies for reducing allocations, shrinking layout sizes, and boosting performance.
25|
26|## Core Rules & Patterns
27|
28|### 1. Bounded Heap-Free Collections
29|For collections that are usually small, avoid standard vectors to bypass heap allocations.
30|- **`SmallVec`**: Stack-allocated up to a threshold, overflows to the heap.
31|- **`ArrayVec`**: Fixed-capacity array wrapper; never allocates on the heap.
32|- **`ThinVec`**: Only takes a single pointer size when empty, reducing size in enum layouts.
33|
34|```rust
35|use smallvec::{smallvec, SmallVec};
36|use arrayvec::ArrayVec;
37|
38|// SmallVec: Allocates 4 items on the stack. Goes to heap only if count > 4.
39|let mut local_tags: SmallVec<[String; 4]> = smallvec![];
40|local_tags.push("Rust".to_string());
41|
42|// ArrayVec: Absolute limit of 8 items on the stack. No heap overflow.
43|let mut coordinates: ArrayVec<f64, 8> = ArrayVec::new();
44|coordinates.push(42.0);
45|```
46|
47|### 2. Small String Optimization (SSO)
48|Standard `String` consumes 24 bytes and allocates heap space immediately. Use `CompactString` for inline small strings (under 24 bytes) without allocating.
49|
50|```rust
51|use compact_str::CompactString;
52|
53|// No heap allocation for strings <= 24 characters
54|let username = CompactString::new("user_123");
55|```
56|
57|### 3. Boxed Slices vs Vectors
58|If a collection's size is determined once at initialization and never changes, convert it from `Vec<T>` to `Box<[T]>` to save 8 bytes of stack capacity space.
59|
60|```rust
61|let items_vec: Vec<i32> = vec![1, 2, 3];
62|
63|// Save capacity field (shrinks stack representation from 24 to 16 bytes)
64|let items_slice: Box<[i32]> = items_vec.into_boxed_slice();
65|```
66|
67|### 4. Zero-Copy Patterns
68|Instead of cloning or allocating strings, hold references to existing memory using slices or crates like `bytes::Bytes`.
69|
70|```rust
71|use bytes::Bytes;
72|
73|pub struct Message {
74|    // Zero-copy reference-counted byte buffer slice
75|    pub payload: Bytes,
76|}
77|
78|// Can be sliced and shared among threads without cloning underlying memory
79|let original = Bytes::from(vec![0; 1024]);
80|let slice = original.slice(0..100); 
81|```
82|
83|### 5. Arena Allocation
84|For batch allocation where structures share a lifecycle (e.g. AST parsing), use arena allocators (`bumpalo`) to allocate items sequentially in a continuous region of memory and free them all at once.
85|
86|```rust
87|use bumpalo::Bump;
88|
89|let bump = Bump::new();
90|
91|// Allocates quickly on the bump arena
92|let string_ref = bump.alloc_str("dynamic string");
93|let int_ref = bump.alloc(42);
94|
95|// Entire arena is cleared at once on drop
96|```
97|
98|### 6. Collection Reuse
99|Reuse collection allocations in performance-critical loops with `.clear()` instead of re-instantiating.
100|
101|```rust
102|// Bad: Allocates a new vector every iteration
103|for item in feed {
104|    let mut batch = Vec::new();
105|    batch.push(item);
106|}
107|
108|// Good: Reuses allocation buffer
109|let mut batch = Vec::with_capacity(100);
110|for item in feed {
111|    batch.clear();
112|    batch.push(item);
113|}
114|```
115|
116|## Layout Awareness
117|
118|Use `std::mem::size_of` to understand data layout.
119|
120|```rust
121|println!("User size: {}", std::mem::size_of::<User>());
122|```
123|
124|Reorder fields to reduce padding only when the type is numerous or hot.
125|
126|```rust
127|// Often smaller: group large-alignment fields first
128|struct Record {
129|    id: u64,
130|    flags: u32,
131|    kind: u8,
132|}
133|```
134|
135|## String Strategy
136|
137|```rust
138|fn label<'a>(name: &'a str, fallback: &'a str) -> std::borrow::Cow<'a, str> {
139|    if name.is_empty() { fallback.into() } else { name.into() }
140|}
141|```
142|
143|Avoid `format!` in tight loops. Reuse buffers with `clear()`.
144|
145|## Zero-Copy Parsing
146|
147|Return slices into the input when the input outlives parsed data.
148|
149|```rust
150|pub struct Header<'a> {
151|    pub name: &'a str,
152|    pub value: &'a str,
153|}
154|```
155|
156|Do not force zero-copy when it creates unmanageable lifetimes for little gain.
157|
158|## ThinVec for Enum Payloads
159|
160|When enums contain `Vec` variants, `ThinVec` reduces the enum size by storing only a pointer when empty:
161|
162|```rust
163|use thin_vec::ThinVec;
164|
165|// Regular Vec in an enum makes the enum 24+ bytes even when empty
166|enum Node {
167|    Leaf(i64),
168|    Children(Vec<Node>),     // 24 bytes for Vec
169|}
170|
171|// ThinVec only stores 8 bytes (a pointer) when empty
172|enum NodeOptimized {
173|    Leaf(i64),
174|    Children(ThinVec<Node>), // 8 bytes for ThinVec
175|}
176|```
177|
178|## Cow for Conditional Ownership
179|
180|```rust
181|use std::borrow::Cow;
182|
183|pub struct Error {
184|    message: Cow<'static, str>,
185|}
186|
187|impl Error {
188|    // No allocation for static messages
189|    pub fn new(msg: &'static str) -> Self {
190|        Self { message: Cow::Borrowed(msg) }
191|    }
192|
193|    // Allocates only when dynamic
194|    pub fn with_detail(msg: String) -> Self {
195|        Self { message: Cow::Owned(msg) }
196|    }
197|}
198|```
199|
200|## Arc vs Rc Trade-offs
201|
202|```rust
203|use std::rc::Rc;
204|use std::sync::Arc;
205|
206|// Single-threaded shared ownership — cheaper than Arc
207|let shared = Rc::new(large_data);
208|
209|// Multi-threaded shared ownership — required across threads
210|let shared = Arc::new(large_data);
211|```
212|
213|Prefer `Rc` when data never crosses thread boundaries. `Arc` adds atomic reference counting overhead.
214|
215|## HashMap Memory Optimization
216|
217|```rust
218|use hashbrown::HashMap;
219|
220|// hashbrown's HashMap uses less memory than std's and is faster
221|let mut map: HashMap<String, i32> = HashMap::with_capacity(128);
222|
223|// Reserve capacity upfront to avoid rehashing
224|map.reserve(expected_count);
225|
226|// Consider FxHashMap for non-adversarial keys
227|use rustc_hash::FxHashMap;
228|let mut fast_map: FxHashMap<String, i32> = FxHashMap::default();
229|```

231|## Stack vs Heap Decision Matrix
232|
233|| Type | Stack Size | Heap Alloc | Use When |
234||------|-----------|------------|----------|
235|| `String` | 24 bytes | Yes | Owns mutable text |
236|| `&str` | 16 bytes | No | Borrowed text, lifetime bound |
237|| `CompactString` | 24 bytes | No (≤24 chars) | Short strings that own data |
238|| `Cow<str>` | 32 bytes | Conditionally | Mostly static, rarely dynamic |
239|| `Box<str>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Owned fixed string |
240|| `Vec<T>` | 24 bytes | Yes | Growable collection |
241|| `SmallVec<[T; N]>` | ~24+ bytes | Only if >N | Usually small, occasionally large |
242|| `Box<[T]>` | 16 bytes | Yes | Fixed-size after construction |
243|| `ThinVec<T>` | 8 bytes | Only if non-empty | Empty or small in enums |
244|
245|## Measuring Memory
246|
247|```rust
248|use std::alloc::{GlobalAlloc, System, Layout};
249|
250|struct TrackingAllocator;
251|
252|unsafe impl GlobalAlloc for TrackingAllocator {
253|    unsafe fn alloc(&self, layout: Layout) -> *mut u8 {
254|        System.alloc(layout)
255|    }
256|

278|
279|## Optimization Workflow
280|
281|1. Measure allocations and CPU first.
282|2. Identify the hot path and expected data sizes.
283|3. Pick the narrowest memory change.
284|4. Benchmark before/after.
285|5. Keep readability unless the win is meaningful.
286|
287|## Allocation Decision Rules
288|
289|- `Vec<T>`: general purpose growable collection.
290|- `SmallVec<[T; N]>`: usually-small collection with occasional heap spill.
291|- `ArrayVec<T, N>`: hard maximum size, no heap allocation.
292|- `Box<[T]>`: fixed-size heap slice after construction.
293|- `Bytes`: shared immutable byte buffers.
294|- `Bump`: many same-lifetime allocations.
295|- `Cow<'a, T>`: borrow unless mutation/ownership is required.
296|
297|## Anti-Patterns
298|
299|```rust
300|// Bad: cloning a large Vec just to avoid lifetime complexity
301|let data = original.clone(); // expensive and unnecessary
302|
303|// Good: use Arc or Cow for shared ownership
304|let data: Arc<[u8]> = original.into();
305|```
306|
307|```rust
308|// Bad: allocating inside a hot loop
309|for item in items {
310|    let s = format!("processing {}", item); // allocates every iteration
311|}
312|
313|// Good: reuse a buffer
314|let mut buf = String::with_capacity(128);
315|for item in items {
316|    buf.clear();
317|    write!(buf, "processing {}", item).unwrap();
318|}
319|```
320|
321|- Replacing every `Vec` with `SmallVec` without measuring.
322|- Keeping arena references after reset.
323|- Cloning strings to satisfy ownership instead of shortening borrow scopes.
324|- Using `Arc` as a default clone workaround.
325|- Optimizing layout for types created a handful of times.
326|- Using `Box<dyn Trait>` when generics would eliminate the allocation entirely.
327|
328|## Review Prompt
329|
330|When reviewing memory optimization, ask what was measured, which allocation is removed, what lifetime assumptions changed, and whether the new type increases stack size or API complexity.
331|
332|## Optimization Checklist
333|
334|- Measure allocations before changing data structures.
335|- Preallocate collections only when capacity is known or bounded.
336|- Prefer borrowing and `Cow` before cloning strings or buffers.
337|- Use arenas only when lifetimes are truly batch-scoped.
338|- Check stack growth when replacing heap allocations with inline storage.
339|- Re-benchmark after changes and keep the simpler version if gains are noise.
340|- Profile with `dhat` or `heaptrack` to find actual allocation hotspots.
341|- Consider `hashbrown` or `rustc-hash` for HashMap-heavy code.

5|
6|# Memory Safety Patterns
7|
8|Cross-language patterns for memory-safe programming including RAII, ownership, smart pointers, and resource management.
9|
10|## When to Use This Skill
11|
12|- Writing memory-safe systems code
13|- Managing resources (files, sockets, memory)
14|- Preventing use-after-free and leaks
15|- Implementing RAII patterns
16|- Choosing between languages for safety
17|- Debugging memory issues
18|
19|## Core Concepts
20|
21|### 1. Memory Bug Categories
22|
23|| Bug Type             | Description                      | Prevention        |
24|| -------------------- | -------------------------------- | ----------------- |
25|| **Use-after-free**   | Access freed memory              | Ownership, RAII   |
26|| **Double-free**      | Free same memory twice           | Smart pointers    |
27|| **Memory leak**      | Never free memory                | RAII, GC          |
28|| **Buffer overflow**  | Write past buffer end            | Bounds checking   |
29|| **Dangling pointer** | Pointer to freed memory          | Lifetime tracking |
30|| **Data race**        | Concurrent unsynchronized access | Ownership, Sync   |
31|
32|### 2. Safety Spectrum
33|
34|```
35|Manual (C) → Smart Pointers (C++) → Ownership (Rust) → GC (Go, Java)
36|Less safe                                              More safe
37|More control                                           Less control
38|```
39|
40|## Detailed patterns and worked examples
41|
42|Detailed pattern documentation lives in `references/details.md`. Read that file when the navigation tier above is insufficient.
43|
44|## Best Practices
45|
46|### Do's
47|
48|- **Prefer RAII** - Tie resource lifetime to scope
49|- **Use smart pointers** - Avoid raw pointers in C++
50|- **Understand ownership** - Know who owns what
51|- **Check bounds** - Use safe access methods
52|- **Use tools** - AddressSanitizer, Valgrind, Miri
53|
54|### Don'ts
55|
56|- **Don't use raw pointers** - Unless interfacing with C
57|- **Don't return local references** - Dangling pointer
58|- **Don't ignore compiler warnings** - They catch bugs
59|- **Don't use `unsafe` carelessly** - In Rust, minimize it
60|- **Don't assume thread safety** - Be explicit
61|
62|## Debugging Tools
63|
64|```bash
65|# AddressSanitizer (Clang/GCC)
66|clang++ -fsanitize=address -g source.cpp
67|
68|# Valgrind
69|valgrind --leak-check=full ./program
70|
71|# Rust Miri (undefined behavior detector)
72|cargo +nightly miri run
73|
74|# ThreadSanitizer
75|clang++ -fsanitize=thread -g source.cpp
76|```

1048|51|FUSE 内核端故障诊断采用**三层下钻模型**，从最外层逐层深入，层间存在依赖关系：
1049|52|
1050|53|```
1051|54|┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
1052|55|│                   三层下钻分析模型                                 │
1053|56|│                                                                 │
1054|57|│   L1: 系统层         mount -t fuse /proc/mounts                 │
1055|58|│       │               /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*                │
1056|59|│       └─ 判断：FUSE 挂载点是否正常？连接是否存在？               │
1057|60|│                                                                 │
1058|61|│   L2: 类型层         strace -p <daemon_pid>                     │
1059|62|│       │               cat /sys/fs/fuse/connections/*/waiting     │
1060|63|│       └─ 判断：是 EIO？请求阻塞？性能退化？权限问题？            │
1061|64|│                                                                 │
1062|65|│   L3: 代码/内核层    FUSE daemon 源码分析                       │
1063|66|│                      内核 FUSE 模块参数 (/sys/module/fuse/)     │
1064|67|│                      /dev/fuse 设备状态                          │
1065|68|│                      └─ 根因定位：daemon 崩溃 / 队列阻塞 / 配置  │
1066|69|│                                                                 │
1067|70|│   每层输出：证据 + 结论。L3 输出最终根因。                       │
1068|71|└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
1069|72|```

{"content":"1|#!/bin/sh
2|# activate-golden.sh — the one command for deploying a new version.
3|#
4|#   sudo ./activate-golden.sh
5|#
6|# Run it after the release build and seal:
7|#   CXXFLAGS="-include cstdint" cargo build --workspace --release
8|#   sudo target/release/opblob seal-shm && sudo target/release/opblob persist
9|# OP_RELEASE_DIR selects one prepared optimized artifact directory for both
10|# release-controller verification and golden preparation (default target/release).
11|#
12|# What it does:
13|# 1. Native provision-slots reconciles any interrupted transaction and prepares
14|#    the owned golden/slot layout. Recovery-only work stops this invocation.
15|# 2. Prepares /opt/op-dbus/golden from target/release and the sealed catalog
16|#    (internal helper deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh; it never builds or seals).
17|# 3. Native release sends/receives the immutable generation into the inactive
18|#    slot, rotates read-only overlays at the inventory's owned host targets,
19|#    and restores affected consumers' wanted states. Only active + previous remain.
20|#
21|# Undo the last release:
22|#   sudo /usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch rollback
23|set -eu
24|PATH=/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
25|LC_ALL=C
26|export PATH LC_ALL
27|
28|REPO=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$(dirname -- "$(readlink -f "$0")")" && pwd)
29|OP_RELEASE_DIR=$(realpath -e -- "${OP_RELEASE_DIR:-"$REPO/target/release"}")
30|export OP_RELEASE_DIR
31|RELEASE_BASE=/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release
32|RELEASE_LAUNCH=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release-launch
33|RELEASE_BIN=$RELEASE_BASE/op-release
34|RELEASE_BOOT=/etc/init.d/op-release-activate
35|
36|[ "$(id -u)" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: run as root (sudo ./activate-golden.sh)' >&2; exit 1; }
37|[ "$#" = 0 ] || { echo 'activate-golden.sh: takes no arguments' >&2; exit 1; }
38|# Check the execution path before invoking any installed kit code. The launcher
39|# independently checks the complete approved manifest and kernel/BTF pair.
40|for directory in / /usr /usr/local /usr/local/libexec "$RELEASE_BASE" /etc /etc/init.d; do
41|    directory_mode=0$(stat -c %a "$directory")
42|    [ -d "$directory" ] && [ ! -L "$directory" ] &&
43|        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g "$directory")" = 0:0 ] &&
44|        [ "$((directory_mode & 07022))" -eq 0 ] ||
45|        { echo "activate-golden.sh: insecure release-kit directory: $directory" >&2; exit 1; }
46|done
47|for artifact in "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$RELEASE_BIN" "$RELEASE_BOOT"; do
48|    [ -f "$artifact" ] && [ ! -L "$artifact" ] &&
49|        [ "$(stat -c %u:%g:%a:%h "$artifact")" = 0:0:755:1 ] ||
50|        { echo "activate-golden.sh: install the approved root-owned release kit: $artifact" >&2; exit 1; }
51|done
52|cmp -s "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-launch" &&
53|    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BIN" "$OP_RELEASE_DIR/op-release" &&
54|    cmp -s "$RELEASE_BOOT" "$REPO/deploy/release/op-release-activate" ||
55|    { echo 'activate-golden.sh: installed release kit differs from this build; refusing an old or mixed kit' >&2; exit 1; }
56|
57|"$RELEASE_LAUNCH" provision-slots
58|"$REPO/deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh"
59|exec "$RELEASE_LAUNCH" release","total_lines":59,"file_size":3008,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

{"content":"1|# Local release activation
2|
3|The current native release controller prepares golden, transfers a read-only
4|snapshot with `btrfs send/receive`, and rotates read-only overlays directly at
5|the inventory's owned host targets. It retains active and previous slots.
6|The older per-file/current-symlink procedures below are historical, not an
7|alternative activation path.
8|
9|## Paths and ownership
10|
11|| Path | Purpose |
12||---|---|
13|| `/opt/op-dbus/golden` | Writable preparation subvolume; never an execution target |
14|| `/opt/op-dbus/release-send/<release-id>` | Immutable source generation used by the native transfer |
15|| Native filesystem roots `@release-a` / `@release-b` | Controller-owned received slots; never populate or select manually |
16|| Inventory-declared host targets | Read-only overlays selected by the activation transaction |
17|| `/var/lib/opdbus-release` | Protected controller state, transaction recovery and first-activation preservation |
18|
19|Retention is configurable per storage owner; there is no global five-subvolume
20|cap. Budget free bytes for preparation, send/receive and a recovery reserve
21|before starting writes. Count paths under the release root explicitly: `btrfs
22|subvolume list -o` on an ordinary directory lists descendants of its
23|containing subvolume, including unrelated Incus storage. Existing unrelated
24|subvolumes are not permission to delete storage. Preserve the category,
25|timing, vector and state subvolumes owned by cache/Snowball. Retain the previous active
26|release for rollback; retire only explicitly identified obsolete releases.
27|
28|## Current entry point and base prerequisites
29|
30|Run `sudo ./activate-golden.sh` from the repository root, preserving the
31|explicit prepared-artifact selectors described below. It validates the
32|independent root-owned release kit, provisions/reconciles slots, prepares
33|golden, then invokes native release/activation. It does not compile or reseal.
34|Use `/usr/local/libexec/opdbus-release/op-release-launch status` for the
35|authoritative slot, journal, overlay and readiness receipt; `rollback` selects
36|the compatible previous release through the same controller.
37|
38|Independent base prerequisites must be ready before the application cutover:
39|
40|- `identity-roots` restores only existing identity-root inventory. An empty
41|  inventory succeeds without provisioning; any failed restoration fails the
42|  service. Login/start/stop never add or remove Btrfs members. Its readiness
43|  marker is emitted only after successful restoration.
44|- On the restored host, the native Open vSwitch package owns its daemons.
45|  The runit `ovsdb-server` service observes the validated native PID with
46|  procps `pidwait`; its bounded check queries the actual Unix socket for
47|  `Open_vSwitch`. It must not launch duplicate daemons, change topology, or
48|  run the old uplink/bootstrap chain. Inspect sockets with native metadata
49|  and protocol tools; a generic directory listing can omit them.
50|- Independent `op-warp-endpoint` restores only the existing declared local
51|  endpoint from `/etc/op-dbus/warp-ssh.json`; `endpoint.sh check` verifies
52|  ownership, address/peer, aliases and MTU. An UP persistent TUN with
53|  NO-CARRIER is not evidence of SSH, remote ingress or authenticated access.
54|  This service does not restore MASQUE, firewall or policy-routing state.
55|- Logger definitions require the existing system `svlog` account/group and
56|  appropriately owned log directories. Long-lived helper services use the
57|  available `sleep infinity`, not an assumed `pause` executable.
58|
59|Runtime TLS, protected capability/toolset policy, provider keys and the
60|production router's matching configuration/token state remain outside the
61|release. The runtime MCP audience and toolset JSON files must be root-owned
62|mode 0600; the bridge rejects group/world-readable policy before binding.
63|Restore missing inputs only from a verified authoritative backup,
64|without printing secret values, overwriting present state, substituting
65|template grants or minting replacement identities. A router token must match
66|the same production gateway's persisted token hash; an unrelated historical
67|configuration is not recovery proof.
68|
69|On this host, `op-storage` and `op-storage-kernel-guard` remain persistently
70|OFF until explicit owner reauthorization. Activation is not permission to
71|rearm them. Enable the independent early-boot release hook only after a
72|successful activation receipt; do not reboot as a deployment check. A
73|received inactive slot is not a deployed application or a mounted 3tchedFS.
74|
75|
76|## Prepare
77|
78|Build the native glibc workspace, prepare its pinned UI and threetched
79|artifacts, and explicitly seal/persist with the freshly built `opblob` and
80|the service's schema-shaping environment. Preserve the previous catalogs and
81|review additions/removals before a live reseal. `build-golden.sh` accepts
82|`OP_PERSISTED_CATALOG_SOURCE` for isolated release preparation.
83|
84|Reuse already-built native binaries by setting `OP_RELEASE_DIR` to the complete
85|prepared executable directory; the default is `target/release`. Set
86|`EMQX_ARTIFACT_CACHE_DIR` and `MCP_PROVIDER_ARTIFACT_CACHE_DIR` when the pinned
87|EMQX archive and nlm wheel are cached outside `/var/cache/op-dbus/source-artifacts`.
88|These selectors do not rebuild binaries or weaken artifact digest checks.
89|The pinned EMQX archive is still digest-verified before extraction. Its unused
90|esockd demonstration private key is excluded from the prepared payload;
91|configured runtime TLS keys remain outside the release at `/etc/emqx/certs`.
92|
93|The execution payload requires GNU Python 3.14. When the host default differs,
94|`OP_EXECUTION_PYTHON_BUNDLE` may name an existing standalone native runtime
95|directory. Preparation copies that runtime into the execution payload, verifies
96|its relocated base prefix, and installs the hash-locked tools into that private
97|prefix. The received release therefore does not depend on a user-managed
98|interpreter under `/home`; the host's default Python is unchanged. Without this
99|selector, preparation retains the native-host virtual-environment path.
100|The preparation receipt records the runtime binary and preparer digests, so a
101|changed interpreter or preparation implementation invalidates reuse.
102|
103|Golden preparation generates the restart inventory from the prepared bytes.
104|Shell assignments are not executable names; quoted substitutions, continuations,
105|declared function arguments and attached redirection paths retain their
106|dependencies without executing the scripts. Captured-source and versioned
107|skill-packaging provenance are classified by their complete JSON structure,
108|not by filename. Unknown executable/configuration references, mixed provenance
109|and configuration records, and absent release inputs still stop preparation.
110|An inventory-helper repair can be built and selected independently; it does
111|not require replacing the existing application binaries or their catalog.
112|
113|When a plugin version changes, rebuild `op-grpc-bridge` from the same plugin
114|source as `opblob` and activate that bridge with the matching catalog. The
115|bridge compares each sealed plugin version and method declaration with its
116|compiled compatibility contract before dispatch. Building only the sealer,
117|even for a description-only version change, leaves the old bridge rejecting
118|calls. Catalog parity and bridge readiness alone do not verify this boundary.
119|
120|Before the workspace build and sealing, select the prepared threetched binary
121|with the paired absolute `THREETCHED_CAPTURE_BIN` and
122|`THREETCHED_CAPTURE_MANIFEST` paths. Keep those selectors identical across both
123|steps; without them discovery uses the installed binary, which may belong to
124|the previous release. The runtime selectors remain `/usr/bin/threetched` and
125|`/usr/share/op-dbus/threetched-manifests/tched-router.json`. Follow the
126|[binary feature preparation procedure](../../../crates/threetched-fs/README.md#add-a-threetched-feature-from-the-binary)
127|for the exact environment, isolated `opblob seal-plugins` invocation, catalog
128|review and mounted verification. Golden preparation rejects mismatched sealed
129|binary or manifest digests.
130|
131|### Provisioning helper payload and ownership
132|
133|Golden includes the provisioning suite in the existing `libexec/3tched`
134|prepared directory. The inventory maps that directory to the read-only host
135|target **`/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers`**, not the base-system
136|`/usr/local/libexec/3tched` directory. Invoke the activated entry point as
137|`/usr/local/libexec/op-dbus/helpers/provision-workspace-subscriber`; scripts
138|are packaged without their source `.sh` suffix and resolve their companion
139|entry points in the same directory.
140|
141|`deploy/lib/golden/build-golden.sh` declares the exact source, destination
142|basename and mode in `RELEASE_HELPER_INPUTS`:
143|
144|| Source under `deploy/` | Packaged helpers/assets |
145|| --- | --- |
146|| `scripts/*.sh` (explicit names only) | `provision-workspace-subscriber`, `prepare-instance-disk`, `sync-instance-upgrade`, `prepare-chatbot-adoption`, `bind-instance-root`, `3tchedfs-invoke` |
147|| `runit/libexec-3tched/` (explicit provisioning dependencies) | `op-identity-root`, `op-identity-image`, `attach-host-workspace-folders`, `restore-chatbot-root` |
148|| `workspace-image/` (offline image inputs) | `prepare-lungs-client` from `prepare-lungs-client.sh`, `3tchedfs-mount-preflight`, `mount.fuse.3tchedFS`, `3tchedfs.service`, `3tchedfs.fstab`, `3tched-lungs.conf` |
149|
150|Executables use mode 0755; the guest service, fstab fragment and tmpfiles
151|configuration use mode 0644. Preparation requires every declared source to
152|be a readable regular non-symlink file; destination modes come from the
153|declaration, not the checkout's executable bits.
154|It copies bytes only; none of these helpers is invoked by golden preparation.
155|The existing application helpers, including the separate host
156|`mount-3tchedfs` adapter, remain included. The guest `mount.fuse.3tchedFS`
157|asset is not installed over the host's mount adapter.
158|
159|The dependency split is deliberate:
160|
161|- The provisioner delegates disk, upgrade, binding and adoption steps to its
162|  packaged siblings. Its legacy physical-seed path also uses

{"content":"1|# Network Operations
2|
3|This page describes **how networking is supposed to work on the current Artix/runit host**, and points at the live inventory when the tree and the machine disagree.
4|
5|For a dated, command-verified snapshot of interfaces, Incus devices, listeners, xray SNI, and mesh forwarders, see:
6|
7|**[Host socket & network topology (live)](host-socket-topology-live.md)**
8|
9|Re-verify that file against the host before topology-changing work (new proxies, prom/graf exposure, socket migrations).
10|
11|## Agent rules and owner decisions (moved from AGENTS.md, 2026-10-14)
12|
13|Read this section before any network, Xray, WARP, decoy, OVS or firewall work.
14|AGENTS.md now only points here.
15|
16|**Partial restoration (2026-10-16).** The native `decoy-admin-reverse-ssh`
17|runit service is restored on the Devuan host using the existing
18|`/home/jeremy/.ssh/decoy_key` and strict host-key checking. The decoy publishes
19|`10.0.0.1:2222` bound to `wg-opdbus`, forwarding to its loopback reverse endpoint;
20|the tunnel terminates at the host's loopback SSH listener. WireGuard terminates
21|only on the decoy, never on this host. A fresh authenticated reverse connection
22|returned `jeremy` on `3tched` and matched the host's authoritative ED25519 key.
23|The external WireGuard-client leg was not exercised from this session.
24|
25|The target layout is eth0 as OVS uplink, pub0 for public addressing (not
26|administrative SSH), two IPv4 addresses on `rtly-lungs` including 10.0.0.2,
27|and three service aliases on ovsbr0 for EMQX, OpenFlow and Qdrant. OVS packages
28|are installed, but no bridge/address/route ownership cutover has occurred.
29|NetworkManager remains active until a protected transfer; afterward it must
30|remain installed but disabled, for emergency recovery only.
31|
32|Owner requests stopping at the application-bridge prerequisite. The existing
33|uplink service waits for `opdbus-rundirs`, which requires `/usr/local/bin/opblob`
34|and a prepared persisted catalog; that executable is absent. This is an
35|application-catalog bootstrap dependency, not proof that the bridge daemon must
36|run to create OVS. Do not bypass it or claim the network cutover is deployed.
37|Public recovery SSH is still enabled: a proposed private-only cutover was
38|reverted when its rollback helper could not execute on the `noexec` `/run`
39|mount. Move forward only with an approved, functioning rollback mechanism.
40|
41|**Current status (2026-10-14).** The host moved from Artix to Devuan 6 (runit:
42|`/etc/sv/<svc>`, enabled via `/etc/runit/runsvdir/default`). Only `eth0`
43|(`188.68.58.237/22`, DHCP) is up; OVS, Incus, Xray and WARP are not installed yet.
44|Owner decision: the network lives on the **base system**, not in a golden release,
45|installed on a new machine by a network preinstall script that pulls these
46|sources from git. The rest of this page, including the GRE description below,
47|predates that move: GRE (`gre-decoy`) and `wgcf` were retired on 2026-10-04 (see
48|`deploy/runit/retired-services`), and `deploy/config/nftables.conf` says SSH
49|transport now uses `tun5`. Xray config/keys and the Xray Incus container are not
50|in git; the recovery disk keeps them under `received/271/root-271/`
51|(`etc/xray`, `var/lib/incus`, `etc/openvswitch`, `etc/nftables.conf`).
52|
53|**Network-critical services.** OVS, uplink, DHCP and the session bus require
54|deliberate operator action; a learning or inventory pass never restarts them.
55|
56|**Xray configuration policy — mandatory.** Xray's live config must exist only at
57|`/etc/xray/xray_config.json` inside the container. Never point Xray at
58|`/dev/shm/xray_config.json`, `/usr/local/etc/xray/config.json`, or any other
59|disk-backed live path. The static bootstrap config is materialized at boot; the
60|future model-generated generator replaces the same file atomically and reloads
61|through D-Bus. Models must not write or reload Xray directly.
62|
63|**Owner-confirmed network topology (2026-09-13).** There is no WireGuard on this
64|server. WireGuard terminates at the decoy; identity is transported by WARP.
65|WireGuard types, plugin declarations, credentials or historical configuration
66|paths in source do not establish a server WireGuard interface or a requirement to
67|install one. Classify those surfaces by their decoy/server role before proposing
68|implementation or retirement. An unwired `wgcf` method is not evidence that the
69|actual WARP identity transport is broken.
70|
71|**Owner decisions: decoy GRE, TLS and identity transport (2026-09-25; GRE since
72|retired).** The door stays `10.0.0.2:8090`: tonic with the internal `svc0`
73|certificate from the op-dbus local CA. The bridge no longer listens on
74|`127.0.0.1:8090` or `10.0.0.3:8090`, and it no longer serves a second browser
75|certificate. Browser-facing TLS terminates on the decoy at `10.0.0.1`. The decoy
76|mints the sealed identity blob, and WARP delivers it to the 8090 interceptor. The
77|oracle (OIA1) is the decoy's signed proof of the WireGuard peer, because
78|WireGuard exists only on the decoy. At the time, the decoy routed browser
79|traffic for `10.0.0.2` over `gre-host` with no WARP route in either main routing
80|table. The `gre-decoy` tunnel joined decoy and host: outer `188.68.58.237` ↔
81|`129.80.64.127`, inner `192.168.255.1/30` plus `10.0.0.2/32`, with `10.0.0.1` and
82|the WireGuard clients `10.0.0.5`–`10.0.0.7` routed via `192.168.255.2`. GRE
83|routing replaced NAT on that path: nftables is the firewall only, never a router,
84|so do not add DNAT, SNAT or masquerade for it. GRE is not encrypted, so anything
85|crossing it that is not TLS is readable on the path. MQTT stays on `10.0.0.3`,
86|aliased on `ovsbr0` beside the OpenFlow address `10.200.0.1`. Xray runs in its
87|container. op-web's page address is `http://10.0.0.4:8080`: plain HTTP outside
88|the TLS zone, with `10.0.0.4/32` on `gre-decoy` and routed from the decoy over
89|`gre-host`. The decoy issuer
90|(`/etc/systemd/system/op-decoy-issuer.service.d/browser-auth.conf` on the decoy,
91|not in this repo) hands out the IP door `https://10.0.0.2:8090` and allows the
92|`10.0.0.4` and `10.0.0.2` page origins; no domain name points browsers at the
93|decoy. Open on 2026-09-25: how the decoy-minted oracle reaches the interceptor
94|(the owner's direction then was over GRE). Until that lands, the deployed page
95|fetches OIA1 from `http://10.0.0.1:51888/identity/self`, and the door rejects a
96|request that carries no credential.
97|
98|## Model in one paragraph
99|
100|One OVS bridge (`ovsbr0`) carries the private fabric. Physical uplink (`eth0`) is enslaved and unaddressed; host L3 lives on OVS internal ports **`pub0`** (public) and **`svc0`** (`10.200.0.2/24`). The **xray** container is the only instance with a NIC on the bridge (`10.200.0.1`). WireGuard mesh interface **`3tched`** (`100.69.0.254/16`) is separate L3 and must never be routed via `ovsbr0`.
101|
102|**Shared socket fabric:** `op-grpc-bridge` dual-listens on host UDS `/run/opdbus/grpc.sock` and shared container UDS `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock` (same gRPC routes). NIC-less containers bind-mount `/run/ghostbridge`. Some services still use Incus TCP proxies / mesh `fwd-*` (migration is incremental).
103|
104|**OpenFlow** (`op-of-controller` on `127.0.0.1:6653`) is intentionally NORMAL/standalone today — reserved for **future tag routing**, not a current blocker for the socket fabric.
105|
106|## Boot order (runit)
107|
108|```text
109|opdbus-rundirs
110|  → uplink-dhcp
111|  → ovsdb-server → ovs-vswitchd
112|  → ovsbr0-uplink → ovsbr0-addr → ovsbr0-svc-addr
113|  → op-of-controller
114|  → wg-3tched
115|  → op-grpc-bridge (cognitive in process) / op-web
116|```
117|
118|Config: `/etc/op-dbus/network.conf`  
119|Helpers: `/usr/local/libexec/3tched/*-up`
120|
121|## Public path
122|
123|Client DNS (NextDNS) → Oracle decoy → WireGuard mesh → host `fwd-8444` → xray SNI on `10.200.0.1:8444` → host services on `10.200.0.2` (dashboard/registration → `:8080`, assistant gRPC → `:8090`, etc.). Live rules: `/dev/shm/xray_config.json` only.
124|
125|## Attachment modes (summary)
126|
127|| Pattern | Used by (live) |
128|| --- | --- |
129|| Bridged NIC on `ovsbr0` | `xray` only |
130|| Shared UDS `/run/ghostbridge/container.sock` | bridge + CT mounts (`assistant`, `qdrant`) |
131|| Incus `proxy` TCP | `mail-3tched`, `netmaker`, `qdrant`, `cozo` |
132|| Mesh `tcpfwd.py` (`fwd-*`) | side channels into xray/host |
133|| Host UDS `/run/opdbus/grpc.sock` | host gRPC clients, session bus |
134|
135|## Do / don't
136|
137|- **Do** check `sudo incus config device show <name>` before assuming UDS-only or proxy-only.
138|- **Do** keep mesh routes on `3tched`; strip accidental `100.69.0.0/16` via `ovsbr0`.
139|- **Do** treat the [Netmaker ACL helper](host-socket-topology-live.md#break-glass-netmaker-acl-recovery) as break-glass recovery; it enables wildcard all-node traffic and bypasses the normal D-Bus path.
140|- **Do not** put `10.200.0.1` on the host.
141|- **Do not** point live xray at `/etc/xray/config.json`.
142|- **Do not** expose Prometheus/Grafana from the netmaker container until the live topology doc is current and the path (mesh vs SNI vs loopback) is chosen.
143|
144|## Stale references
145|
146|Older address tables and dinit/ens3 socket-port writeups under `docs/network-address-table.md` and `docs/operations/ghostbridge-incus-ovs-architecture.md` describe previous hosts or intent. Prefer the live topology snapshot and this page for the 2026-07 Artix/runit host.","total_lines":146,"file_size":9175,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

{"content":"1|#!/bin/sh
2|# Internal reverse endpoint:
3|# decoy 127.0.0.1:2222 -> this host 127.0.0.1:22.
4|# The decoy's op-main-ssh-wg.socket publishes that endpoint only on
5|# 10.0.0.1%wg-opdbus:2222. It replaces Netmaker for administration and never
6|# establishes OIA1 application identity.
7|exec 2>&1
8|
9|PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin
10|export PATH
11|DECOY_HOST=129.80.64.127
12|
13|network_ready() {
14|    route=$(ip -4 route get "$DECOY_HOST" 2>/dev/null) || return 1
15|    case "$route" in *linkdown*) return 1 ;; esac
16|    iface=$(printf '%s\n' "$route" | awk '{for (i=1; i<NF; i++) if ($i == "dev") {print $(i+1); exit}}')
17|    [ -n "$iface" ] || return 1
18|    [ "$(cat "/sys/class/net/$iface/carrier" 2>/dev/null)" = 1 ]
19|}
20|
21|if ! network_ready; then
22|    echo "decoy-admin-reverse-ssh: waiting for a usable route to $DECOY_HOST"
23|    until network_ready; do
24|        sleep 5
25|    done
26|fi
27|
28|echo "decoy-admin-reverse-ssh: connecting to $DECOY_HOST:22"
29|exec chpst -u jeremy:jeremy /usr/bin/ssh -NT \
30|  -F /dev/null \
31|  -i /home/jeremy/.ssh/decoy_key \
32|  -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
33|  -o BatchMode=yes \
34|  -o ConnectTimeout=10 \
35|  -o ConnectionAttempts=1 \
36|  -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
37|  -o ServerAliveInterval=15 \
38|  -o ServerAliveCountMax=3 \
39|  -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes \
40|  -R 127.0.0.1:2222:127.0.0.1:22 \
41|  "ubuntu@$DECOY_HOST"","total_lines":41,"file_size":1332,"truncated":false,"is_binary":false,"is_image":false,"not_found":false}

**Confirmed: the boot error is misleading. AppArmor is compiled into this kernel but omitted from its active LSM list. It is not a missing Incus profile or an actual privilege denial.**

### Exact evidence
Current boot: **2026-10-18 22:13:10 UTC**, boot ID `13f82f92-1d8c-49b2-92a0-eb856c536ea8`; kernel `6.18.57-x64v3-op-release-lifetime1-xanmod1`.

- `/var/log/boot:24`:
  ```text
  Sun Oct 18 18:13:14 2026: Starting: AppArmorLoading AppArmor profiles - failed, Do you have the correct privileges? ... failed!
  ```
  This boot logger uses UTC−04:00: **22:13:14 UTC**.
- Current kernel ring buffer:
  ```text
  2026-10-18T22:13:11,257551+00:00 LSM: initializing lsm=capability,landlock,lockdown,yama,bpf
  ```
- `/var/log/runit/incus/current:4–5`, **22:13:30 UTC**, `incusd` PID **2038**:
  ```text
  AppArmor support has been disabled because of lack of kernel support
   - AppArmor support has been disabled, Disabled because of lack of kernel support
  ```

### Root cause and impact
- `/boot/config-6.18.57-x64v3-op-release-lifetime1-xanmod1:9165,9212–9213`:
  ```text
  CONFIG_SECURITY_APPARMOR=y
  CONFIG_DEFAULT_SECURITY_DAC=y
  CONFIG_LSM="landlock,lockdown,yama,integrity,bpf"
  ```
  Repository `deploy/release/lifetime/native.config:11628` has the same omission.
- Current `/proc/cmdline` has **no** `lsm=`, `security=`, or `apparmor=` override. Older `apparmor=0` entries in `kern.log` belong to earlier boots.
- `/sys/module/apparmor/parameters/enabled` is **N**. Securityfs **is mounted**, but `/sys/kernel/security/apparmor` does not exist.
- Runit stage 1 invokes `/etc/rcS.d/S12apparmor`. Its library mistakes `/sys/module/apparmor` existence for availability, then reports “correct privileges?” when the nonexistent `.load` file fails its writability check: `/lib/apparmor/rc.apparmor.functions:60–63,175–186,203–218`.
- Incus’s loader correctly skips loading because its mount-mediation feature file is absent (`/usr/libexec/incus/incus-apparmor-load:6–14`). `/etc/apparmor.d/lxc-containers` **exists**. No individual profile failed parsing.

**Incus remains running, but AppArmor confinement is unavailable host-wide.** This is not merely harmless missing-profile noise. No current-boot AppArmor `DENIED` events were found; that does not prove confinement health when the LSM is inactive. Audit initialized disabled, and `/var/log/audit/audit.log` is historical (last modified October 9).

The adjacent Incus “kernel/BTF requires guard policy review” warning is a **separate guard-bootstrap issue**, not the AppArmor cause.

### Smallest safe recommendation
For a separately authorized maintenance boot, enable AppArmor in the existing LSM chain **without removing BPF or other entries**—a candidate boot override is:
```text
lsm=landlock,lockdown,yama,integrity,apparmor,bpf
```
No kernel rebuild appears necessary. Review boot configuration and policy compatibility first; after reboot verify active LSMs, loaded enforcing profiles and Incus confinement. Do not suppress this by disabling the boot loader, changing permissions, or using complain mode. Preserve the existing storage-guard hold.

**No files or runtime state changed; no reload/restart/tests performed.** One ordinary-user Incus-log metadata read was denied; no retry/bypass was attempted. Authorized privileged log reads had already succeeded.

Two partitions, yes:

  1. Root partition: the identity’s writable Btrfs leaf attached to the read-only seed.
  2. Upgrade partition: a separate Btrfs filesystem with its own @ subvolume.

{"content":"1|#!/usr/bin/env bash

7|action=$1 name=$2
8|[[ $(id -u) == 0 ]] || fail 'host root required'
9|# Restoration uses the existing native/storage receipts below, not an online
10|# preparation replay; the bridge may itself depend on this root at boot.

15|readback() { timeout --kill-after=5s 15s "$@"; }

18|stat() { readback stat "$@"; }

{"success":true,"name":"google-workspace","description":"Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets via gws CLI or Python.","tags":["Google","Gmail","Calendar","Drive","Sheets","Docs","Contacts","Email","OAuth"],"related_skills":["himalaya"],"content":"--- name: google-workspace description: "Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets via gws CLI or Python." version: 1.2.0 author: Nous Research license: MIT platforms: [linux, macos, windows] required_credential_files: - path: google_token.json description: Google OAuth2 token (created by setup script) - path: google_client_secret.json description: Google OAuth2 client credentials (downloaded from Google Cloud Console) metadata: hermes: tags: [Google, Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Sheets, Docs, Contacts, Email, OAuth] homepage: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent related_skills: [himalaya] --- # Google Workspace Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Contacts, Sheets, and Docs — through Hermes-managed OAuth and a thin CLI wrapper. When `gws` is installed, the skill uses it as the execution backend for broader Google Workspace coverage; otherwise it falls back to the bundled Python client implementation. ## References - `references/gmail-search-syntax.md` — Gmail search operators (is:unread, from:, newer_than:, etc.) - `references/daily-brief.md` — daily/morning brief procedure: schedule + conflicts + meeting prep + urgent mail from Gmail and Calendar. Load it when the user asks for a morning brief, meeting preparation, or "what's on my calendar and what email needs attention." ## Scripts - `scripts/setup.py` — OAuth2 setup (run once to authorize) - `scripts/google_api.py` — compatibility wrapper CLI. It prefers `gws` for operations when available, while preserving Hermes' existing JSON output contract. ## First-Time Setup The setup is fully non-interactive — you drive it step by step so it works on CLI, Telegram, Discord, or any platform. Run the setup script with Python from the Hermes environment, not an unrelated system Python. `--install-deps` syncs Hermes' declared Google extra through PM; after syncing, restart Hermes and rerun the OAuth command. If Hermes is not importable, use `hermes setup` first rather than installing packages with pip. Define a shorthand first: ```bash GSETUP="python ${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/productivity/google-workspace/scripts/setup.py" ``` ### Step 0: Check if already set up ```bash $GSETUP --check ``` If it prints `AUTHENTICATED`, skip to Usage — setup is already done. ### Step 1: Triage — ask the user what they need Before starting OAuth setup, ask the user TWO questions: **Question 1: "What Google services do you need? Just email, or also Calendar/Drive/Sheets/Docs?"** - **Email only** → They don't need this skill at all. Use the `himalaya` skill instead — it works with a Gmail App Password (Settings → Security → App Passwords) and takes 2 minutes to set up. No Google Cloud project needed. Load the himalaya skill and follow its setup instructions. - **Email + Calendar** → Continue with this skill, but use `--services email,calendar` during auth so the consent screen only asks for the scopes they actually need. - **Calendar/Drive/Sheets/Docs only** → Continue with this skill and use a narrower `--services` set like `calendar,drive,sheets,docs`. - **Full Workspace access** → Continue with this skill and use the default `all` service set. **Question 2: "Does your Google account use Advanced Protection (hardware security keys required to sign in)? If you're not sure, you probably don't — it's something you would have explicitly enrolled in."** - **No / Not sure** → Normal setup. Continue below. - **Yes** → Their Workspace admin must add the OAuth client ID to the org's allowed apps list before Step 4 will work. Let them know upfront. ### Step 2: Create OAuth credentials (one-time, ~5 minutes) Tell the user: > You need a Google Cloud OAuth client. This is a one-time setup: > > 1. Create or select a project: > https://console.cloud.google.com/projectselector2/home/dashboard > 2. Enable the required APIs from the API Library: > https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library > Enable: Gmail API, Google Calendar API, Google Drive API, > Google Sheets API, Google Docs API, People API > 3. Create the OAuth client here: > https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials > Credentials → Create Credentials → OAuth 2.0 Client ID > 4. Application type: "Desktop app" → Create > 5. If the app is still in Testing, add the user's Google account as a test user here: > https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience > Audience → Test users → Add users > 6. Download the JSON file and tell me the file path > > Important Hermes CLI note: if the file path starts with `/`, do NOT send only the bare path as its own message in the CLI, because it can be mistaken for a slash command. Send it in a sentence instead, like: > `The JSON file path is: ~/Downloads/client_secret_....json` Once they provide the path: ```bash $GSETUP --client-secret /path/to/client_secret.json ``` If they paste the raw client ID / client secret values instead of a file path, write a valid Desktop OAuth JSON file for them yourself, save it somewhere explicit (for example `~/Downloads/hermes-google-client-secret.json`), then run `--client-secret` against that file. ### Step 3: Get authorization URL Use the service set chosen in Step 1. Examples: ```bash $GSETUP --auth-url --services email,calendar --format json $GSETUP --auth-url --services calendar,drive,sheets,docs --format json $GSETUP --auth-url --services all --format json ``` This returns JSON with an `auth_url` field and also saves the exact URL to `~/.hermes/google_oauth_last_url.txt`. Agent rules for this step: - Extract the `auth_url` field and send that exact URL to the user as a single line. - Tell the user that the browser will likely fail on `http://localhost:1` after approval, and that this is expected. - Tell them to copy the ENTIRE redirected URL from the browser address bar. - If the user gets `Error 403: access_denied`, send them directly to `https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience` to add themselves as a test user. ### Step 4: Exchange the code The user will paste back either a URL like `http://localhost:1/?code=4/0A...&scope=...` or just the code string. Either works. The `--auth-url` step stores a temporary pending OAuth session locally so `--auth-code` can complete the PKCE exchange later, even on headless systems: ```bash $GSETUP --auth-code "THE_URL_OR_CODE_THE_USER_PASTED" --format json ``` If `--auth-code` fails because the code expired, was already used, or came from an older browser tab, it now returns a fresh `fresh_auth_url`. In that case, immediately send the new URL to the user and have them retry with the newest browser redirect only. ### Step 5: Verify ```bash $GSETUP --check ``` Should print `AUTHENTICATED`. Setup is complete — token refreshes automatically from now on. ### Notes - Token is stored at `~/.hermes/google_token.json` and auto-refreshes. - Pending OAuth session state/verifier are stored temporarily at `~/.hermes/google_oauth_pending.json` until exchange completes. - If `gws` is installed, `google_api.py` points it at the same `~/.hermes/google_token.json` credentials file. Users do not need to run a separate `gws auth login` flow. - To revoke: `$GSETUP --revoke` ## Usage All commands go through the API script. Set `GAPI` as a shorthand: ```bash GAPI="python ${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/productivity/google-workspace/scripts/google_api.py" ``` ### Gmail ```bash # Search (returns JSON array with id, from, subject, date, snippet) $GAPI gmail search "is:unread" --max 10 $GAPI gmail search "from:boss@company.com newer_than:1d" $GAPI gmail search "has:attachment filename:pdf newer_than:7d" # Read full message (returns JSON with body text) $GAPI gmail get MESSAGE_ID # Send $GAPI gmail send --to user@example.com --subject "Hello" --body "Message text" $GAPI gmail send --to user@example.com --subject "Report" --body "

Q4

Details...

" --html $GAPI gmail send --to user@example.com --subject "Hello" --from '"Research Agent" ' --body "Message text" # Reply (automatically threads and sets In-Reply-To) $GAPI gmail reply MESSAGE_ID --body "Thanks, that works for me." $GAPI gmail reply MESSAGE_ID --from '"Support Bot" ' --body "Thanks" # Labels $GAPI gmail labels $GAPI gmail modify MESSAGE_ID --add-labels LABEL_ID $GAPI gmail modify MESSAGE_ID --remove-labels UNREAD ``` ### Calendar ```bash # List events (defaults to next 7 days) $GAPI calendar list $GAPI calendar list --start 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z --end 2026-03-07T23:59:59Z # Create event (ISO 8601 with timezone required) $GAPI calendar create --summary "Team Standup" --start 2026-03-01T10:00:00-06:00 --end 2026-03-01T10:30:00-06:00 $GAPI calendar create --summary "Lunch" --start 2026-03-01T12:00:00Z --end 2026-03-01T13:00:00Z --location "Cafe" $GAPI calendar create --summary "Review" --start 2026-03-01T14:00:00Z --end 2026-03-01T15:00:00Z --attendees "alice@co.com,bob@co.com" # Delete event $GAPI calendar delete EVENT_ID ``` ### Drive ```bash # Search existing files $GAPI drive search "quarterly report" --max 10 $GAPI drive search "mimeType='application/pdf'" --raw-query --max 5 # Get metadata for a single file $GAPI drive get FILE_ID # Upload a local file (auto-detects MIME type) $GAPI drive upload /path/to/report.pdf $GAPI drive upload /path/to/image.png --name "Logo.png" --parent FOLDER_ID # Download (binary files download as-is; Google-native files export to a # sensible default — Docs→pdf, Sheets→csv, Slides→pdf, Drawings→png) $GAPI drive download FILE_ID $GAPI drive download DOC_ID --output ~/doc.pdf $GAPI drive download DOC_ID --export-mime text/plain --output ~/doc.txt # Create a folder $GAPI drive create-folder "Reports" $GAPI drive create-folder "Q4" --parent FOLDER_ID # Share $GAPI drive share FILE_ID --email alice@example.com --role reader $GAPI drive share FILE_ID --email alice@example.com --role writer --notify $GAPI drive share FILE_ID --type anyone --role reader # anyone with link $GAPI drive share FILE_ID --type domain --domain example.com --role reader # Delete — defaults to trash (reversible). Use --permanent to skip the trash. $GAPI drive delete FILE_ID $GAPI drive delete FILE_ID --permanent ``` ### Contacts ```bash $GAPI contacts list --max 20 ``` ### Sheets ```bash # Create a new spreadsheet $GAPI sheets create --title "Q4 Budget" $GAPI sheets create --title "Inventory" --sheet-name "Stock" # Read $GAPI sheets get SHEET_ID "Sheet1!A1:D10" # Write $GAPI sheets update SHEET_ID "Sheet1!A1:B2" --values '[["Name","Score"],["Alice","95"]]' # Append rows $GAPI sheets append SHEET_ID "Sheet1!A:C" --values '[["new","row","data"]]' ``` ### Docs ```bash # Read (a tabbed Doc returns a "tabs" array; single-tab and legacy Docs also return "body") $GAPI docs get DOC_ID $GAPI docs get DOC_ID --tab TAB_ID # read one tab of a tabbed Doc # Create a new Doc (optionally seeded with body text) $GAPI docs create --title "Meeting Notes" $GAPI docs create --title "Draft" --body "First paragraph..." # Append text to the end of an existing Doc $GAPI docs append DOC_ID --text "Additional content to append" $GAPI docs append DOC_ID --tab TAB_ID --text "..." # --tab required when the Doc has multiple tabs ``` ## Output Format All commands return JSON. Parse with `jq` or read directly. Key fields: - **Gmail search**: `[{id, threadId, from, to, subject, date, snippet, labels}]` - **Gmail get**: `{id, threadId, from, to, subject, date, labels, body}` - **Gmail send/reply**: `{status: "sent", id, threadId}` - **Calendar list**: `[{id, summary, start, end, location, description, htmlLink}]` - **Calendar create**: `{status: "created", id, summary, htmlLink}` - **Drive search**: `[{id, name, mimeType, modifiedTime, webViewLink}]` - **Drive get**: `{id, name, mimeType, modifiedTime, size, webViewLink, parents, owners}` - **Drive upload**: `{status: "uploaded", id, name, mimeType, webViewLink}` - **Drive download**: `{status: "downloaded", id, name, path, mimeType}` - **Drive create-folder**: `{status: "created", id, name, webViewLink}` - **Drive share**: `{status: "shared", permissionId, fileId, role, type}` - **Drive delete**: `{status: "trashed" | "deleted", fileId, permanent}` - **Contacts list**: `[{name, emails: [...], phones: [...]}]` - **Sheets get**: `[[cell, cell, ...], ...]` - **Sheets create**: `{status: "created", spreadsheetId, title, spreadsheetUrl}` - **Docs create**: `{status: "created", documentId, title, url}` - **Docs append**: `{status: "appended", documentId, inserted_at, characters}` ## Rules 1. **Never send email, create/delete calendar events, delete Drive files, share files, or modify Docs/Sheets without confirming with the user first.** Show what will be done (recipients, file IDs, content, share role) and ask for approval. For `drive delete`, prefer the default trash (reversible) over `--permanent`. 2. **Check auth before first use** — run `setup.py --check`. If it fails, guide the user through setup. 3. **Use the Gmail search syntax reference** for complex queries — load it with `skill_view("google-workspace", file_path="references/gmail-search-syntax.md")`. 4. **Calendar times must include timezone** — always use ISO 8601 with offset (e.g., `2026-03-01T10:00:00-06:00`) or UTC (`Z`). 5. **Respect rate limits** — avoid rapid-fire sequential API calls. Batch reads when possible. ## Troubleshooting | Problem | Fix | |---------|-----| | `NOT_AUTHENTICATED` | Run setup Steps 2-5 above | | `REFRESH_FAILED` | Token revoked or expired — redo Steps 3-5 | | `HttpError 403: Insufficient Permission` | Missing API scope — `$GSETUP --revoke` then redo Steps 3-5 | | `AUTHENTICATED (partial)` or "Token missing scopes" | New write capabilities (Drive write/delete, Docs create/edit) require re-authorization. `$GSETUP --revoke` then redo Steps 3-5 to grant the upgraded scopes. | | `HttpError 403: Access Not Configured` | API not enabled — user needs to enable it in Google Cloud Console | | `ModuleNotFoundError` | Run `$GSETUP --install-deps` | | Advanced Protection blocks auth | Workspace admin must allowlist the OAuth client ID | ## Revoking Access ```bash $GSETUP --revoke ``` ","path":"productivity/google-workspace/SKILL.md","skill_dir":"/home/jeremy/.hermes/skills/productivity/google-workspace","linked_files":{"references":["references/daily-brief.md","references/gmail-search-syntax.md"],"scripts":["scripts/_hermes_home.py","scripts/google_api.py","scripts/gws_bridge.py","scripts/setup.py"]},"usage_hint":"To view linked files, call skill_view(name, file_path) where file_path is e.g. 'references/api.md' or 'assets/config.yaml'","required_environment_variables":[],"required_commands":[],"missing_required_environment_variables":[],"missing_credential_files":["google_token.json","google_client_secret.json"],"missing_required_commands":[],"setup_needed":true,"setup_skipped":false,"readiness_status":"setup_needed","_source_path":"/home/jeremy/.hermes/skills/productivity/google-workspace/SKILL.md","setup_note":"Setup needed before using this skill: missing file google_token.json, file google_client_secret.json.","metadata":{"hermes":{"tags":["Google","Gmail","Calendar","Drive","Sheets","Docs","Contacts","Email","OAuth"],"homepage":"https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent","related_skills":["himalaya"]}}}
